facts.statement: The researchers investigated whether treating bone marrow cells with EGF could protect against brain damage in a rat model of neurodegeneration.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Forty rats were divided into four groups: a control group, a group with induced injury, a group receiving standard cells, and a group receiving cells treated with EGF.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Brain injury was simulated in the rats by administering a chemical called trimethyltin chloride.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Scientists measured how well the rats learned and moved, examined brain tissue under a microscope, and checked levels of specific proteins and genes.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: In lab dishes, cells treated with 10 ng/mL of EGF survived just as well as normal cells but grew into shapes resembling neurons.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Rats receiving the EGF-treated cells showed better memory and movement skills than those receiving no treatment or just the untreated cells.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Microscopic examination showed that the brain structures in the hippocampus were better preserved in rats treated with the EGF-modified cells.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The treatment lowered markers of inflammation and nerve damage while raising levels of factors that support nerve growth and repair.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The authors conclude that this approach might be a promising future treatment for neurodegenerative diseases, though it is currently based on animal findings.
facts.subject: animals
